exam: A 9‑year‑old boy presents with chronic cough and weight loss. His BMI‑for‑age is below the 5th percentile. What is the most likely diagnosis and first investigation? — TB screening (sputum X‑pert) and nutritional assessment; treat TB and provide therapeutic feeding.

A 14‑year‑old girl has a BMI‑for‑age of 98th percentile and elevated fasting glucose. What is the next step in management? — Screen for insulin resistance, advise diet and exercise, consider metformin if lifestyle fails.
During a ward round you notice a child with a BMI of 30 kg/m². What red flag should prompt urgent referral? — Hypertension or cardiac murmurs indicating early cardiovascular risk.
A child with severe acute malnutrition is being re‑fed. Which drug should be avoided and why? — Paracetamol in high doses can cause hepatotoxicity; use low‑dose paracetamol only if needed.

You are in a rural clinic with no laboratory. A child has a BMI <5th percentile and recurrent diarrhoea. What is the most appropriate management? — Start therapeutic feeding (RUTF), give zinc and vitamin A, and treat diarrhoea with ORS.

A 10‑year‑old with obesity shows normal waist circumference but high blood pressure. What explains this? — Early hypertension can precede central obesity; screen for renal disease and counsel on lifestyle.
ai.title: Body Mass Index in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. In children it is interpreted against age‑ and sex‑specific charts. It helps identify under‑nutrition, stunting, wasting and obesity, guiding management in low‑resource settings.

b: Weight measured with a calibrated scale
Height measured with a stadiometer or length board
sections.p: BMI is calculated as weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². For children, the result is plotted on WHO or CDC BMI‑for‑age growth charts to determine percentiles or z‑scores.

Children are classified by BMI‑for‑age percentiles: under‑weight (<5th), normal (5th–85th), overweight (85th–95th), obese (≥95th). In adults, WHO cut‑offs are <18.5 under‑weight, 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, ≥30 obese.

In low‑resource settings, under‑nutrition stems from food insecurity, infections (malaria, HIV, TB), diarrhoea, and micronutrient deficiencies. Over‑weight/obesity is increasingly linked to urbanisation, processed foods, and sedentary lifestyles.
Under‑weight children may appear thin, with stunted growth and delayed milestones. Over‑weight/obese children may have excess fat, central obesity, and early signs of insulin resistance.
BMI is a screening tool; further tests depend on clinical context.

t.b: Low MUAC suggests wasting and higher mortality risk
Low Hb indicates iron deficiency or chronic disease

sections.p: Severe under‑nutrition can lead to impaired immunity, growth failure, and developmental delay. Obesity increases risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and psychosocial issues.

b: Re‑feeding protocols for severe acute malnutrition
sections.p: Treat underlying causes first: nutritional rehabilitation, infection control, and micronutrient supplementation. Supportive care includes monitoring growth and weight gain.
Regular growth monitoring, community nutrition education, and early screening for infections reduce morbidity.
BMI is not a direct measure of body fat; it can misclassify muscular children as overweight. Body composition assessment (e.g., skinfolds) is needed for accurate fat estimation.
In oedematous states (edema, ascites) weight is inflated, giving a falsely high BMI. In severe stunting, height is low, potentially over‑estimating BMI.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe wasting (weight <70% of median for age)
Signs of infection (fever, cough, diarrhoea) in under‑weight child
Hypertension or cardiac symptoms in obese child
